notes: Asylum social-group causation after Quijano and Shah; IAT decision affirmed on family persecution route.

enrichment.short_title: Family asylum claim fails where persecution targets primary victim only

statutes_considered.title: Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees 1951

key_facts: The appellant, an Iranian national, claimed asylum after alleged persecution linked to her royalist family and her detained husband.
The adjudicator allowed the appeal on asylum and Article 3 grounds, finding a serious risk of detention and ill-treatment if returned.
The IAT allowed the Secretary of State's appeal because the husband's detention was not shown to be for a Convention reason, applying Quijano.
Permission to appeal was granted on whether Quijano remained good law after Shah and Islam.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Immigration Appeal Tribunal reversing an adjudicator's allowance of asylum and human rights claims.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Quijano held still binding; family-member persecution arising from a non-Convention primary target does not establish refugee status.
enrichment.ratio: Where a family member is persecuted only as a means of getting at another person persecuted for a non-Convention reason, the feared persecution is not 'for reasons of' membership of a particular social group; Shah does not overturn Quijano on causation, and the persecutor's end rather than incidental family connection determines Convention protection.
legal_issues: Whether family members persecuted because of a relative's non-Convention persecution qualify as refugees
Whether Quijano survives Shah and Islam
Meaning of 'particular social group' and causation under Article 1A(2)
linked_authorities: Quijano [1997] IAR 227
Shah and Islam [1999] 2 AC 629
de Mello [1997] IAR 43
Skenderaj [2002] EWCA Civ 567
Sarrazola [2000] FCA 919

confidence.notes: Legal analysis is extensive and unanimous. Factual findings at adjudicator level are largely accepted.

notes: Part 20 trust appeal only; trustee breach does not bar account against transferee is the live ratio.

enrichment.short_title: Trustee in breach may still account from nominee transferee
key_facts: Orion held Micro Group shares as nominee for Montrose and the Leat Investors; Montrose's beneficial interest was 100,000 ordinary and 50,000 preference shares.
Without Montrose's consent, Orion exchanged Heapdawn shares for Birchall shares and arranged for Richard Upton to hold them, breaching trust twice.
Montrose's interest was transmuted into a minority Birchall stake and sale proceeds of £4,975,000 were paid to Upton.
The judge held Orion could not sue Upton because of Orion's own breach; the Court of Appeal reversed on the Part 20 claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on the Part 20 issue only after compromise of the main breach-of-trust appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on Part 20 claim; account ordered as between Orion and Upton.
enrichment.ratio: A trustee's breach of trust vis-à-vis its beneficiary does not divest the trustee of its right to recover trust property or proceeds from a transferee; where trust assets were wrongfully transferred through a further nominee, the transferee who knew of Orion's claim before distribution must account to the trustee.
legal_issues: Whether Orion's breach of trust precluded a claim against Upton
Whether Upton held proceeds for the Leat Investors alone
Whether resulting or constructive trust analysis was required

confidence.notes: Live issue is narrow and clearly resolved. Underlying fact pattern is complex and partly compromised.

notes: TCC preliminary issues on alleged direct engagement and tripartite direct-payment agreement; factual dispute resolved against subcontractor.

enrichment.short_title: No direct Canary Wharf contract beyond £25,000 payment mechanism
key_facts: PC Partitions subcontracted ceiling and partition works at HQ5 from IES to CWC on the Clifford Chance fit-out.
After payment difficulties, a March 2003 meeting addressed PCP's cash flow; CWC issued a £25,000 provisional purchase order.
PCP claimed CWC directly engaged it for all subsequent works; CWC said only a direct-payment mechanism applied to variations.
A tripartite Direct Payment Agreement dated 20 June 2003 provided for CWC to pay PCP directly for agreed variation sums only.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of preliminary issues on alleged CWC Agreement, representations, and tripartite Direct Payment Agreement before main quantum claim.
enrichment.outcome: Preliminary issues decided for CWC: only a limited £25,000 on-account payment agreement; no relevant representation; Direct Payment Agreement effective on its express terms; no restitutionary work requests.
enrichment.ratio: Contemporaneous documents showing continued IES subcontracting and valuations undermine an alleged oral direct contract with the main contractor; a later tripartite direct-payment agreement validly limited CWC's direct payment obligations to variations and excluded third-party enforcement rights without implying additional terms.
legal_issues: Whether a concluded direct engagement agreement was made at the March 2003 meeting
Whether the Direct Payment Agreement bound PCP and excluded direct claims
Whether implied terms or UCTA rendered clauses 6 and 12 unenforceable
Whether circumstances amounted to requests giving rise to restitution

notes: Post-trial patent costs order after split validity outcome; issue-based CPR 44.3 apportionment.

enrichment.short_title: Issue-based patent costs after partial invalidity success
key_facts: Following a June 2004 judgment, claims 1 and 2 of the Bromcom patent were invalid for lack of inventive step over Kingshurst but claim 7 remained valid.
Neither party sought leave to appeal the merits judgment.
The two-week trial involved numerous validity attacks, many unsuccessful, including SIMS, SYMBOL, documentary art, and EARS prior use.
The court apportioned trial time by issue to determine net costs after reserved interlocutory applications.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Argument on order terms and costs after split patent validity judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Claimant ordered to pay defendant 8% of reasonable costs net of specified reserved-cost adjustments; no order for costs of the costs hearing.
enrichment.ratio: Under CPR 44.3, where both parties succeed on distinct patent validity issues, costs may be apportioned by issue and percentage of trial time; a party successful on invalidity does not generally recover costs of failed validity attacks unless tied to successful objections, and an exceptional case may require a generally successful party to pay costs on issues lost without proof of unreasonable conduct.
legal_issues: Correct principles for apportioning patent trial costs after partial success
Whether failed validity grounds should carry separate costs orders
Treatment of reserved costs of evidential and experimental applications
linked_authorities: Apotex Europe Ltd v Smith Kline Beecham [2004] EWHC 964 (Ch)
Summit Property Ltd v Pitmans [2001] EWCA Civ 2020
Phonographic Performance Ltd v AIE Rediffusion Ltd [1991] 1 WLR 1507
Johnson Estates (1990) Ltd v Secretary of State for the Environment [2001] EWCA Civ 6535

confidence.notes: Costs reasoning is clear though percentage apportionment is necessarily broad. Merits validity findings are taken from the earlier judgment.

notes: Youth court mode-of-trial JR; Camberwell Green applied to quash Crown Court committal.

enrichment.short_title: Youth court could not reopen retained s20 jurisdiction
key_facts: The claimant, born April 1987, faced section 18 and section 20 OAPA charges with a co-defendant.
On 26 November 2003 the youth court committed the section 18 matter to the Crown Court but retained section 20 for trial in the youth court after not guilty pleas.
On 22 March 2004 the court recommitted the section 20 charge to the Crown Court, treating the November decision as not a determination.
The claimant sought judicial review, arguing the youth court lacked power to reopen its earlier mode-of-trial decision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of youth court decision to commit for trial on section 20 after earlier decision to retain jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Application granted; decision to commit the claimant for trial on section 20 quashed.
enrichment.ratio: A magistrates' court makes a single mode-of-trial decision and cannot reopen it outside section 25; where section 25 does not apply to a section 20 offence because it is not a grave offence under section 91, an erroneous earlier retention decision remains binding and a later committal is unlawful.
legal_issues: Whether a decision to retain youth court jurisdiction had been made on 26 November 2003
Whether the youth court could reconsider venue outside section 25
Whether section 25 applied to a non-grave section 20 charge
linked_authorities: R (DPP) v Camberwell Green Youth Court (5 December 2003)

confidence.notes: Statutory analysis and outcome are straightforward and closely follow Camberwell Green.

notes: Planning JR on PPG6 town-centre classification; Policy S2 held not to define town centre boundary.

enrichment.short_title: Local Plan shopping policy area did not define town centre

statutes_considered.title: Planning Policy Guidance 6: Town Centres and Retail Developments

key_facts: Rushcliffe granted outline planning permission for a c.1,000 sq m net food store at The Manor public house, West Bridgford.
The Co-operative Group, operating a nearby store, challenged the decision by judicial review.
The council treated the site as within the town centre so no need demonstration was required under PPG6.
The claimant argued Policy S2 of the adopted local plan defined the town centre and the site lay outside it.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of planning permission on town-centre classification and retail policy grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; permission upheld; claimant ordered to pay council costs of £10,033 and second interested party costs of £2,646.69.
enrichment.ratio: Policy S2 regulates main shopping frontage uses and does not define the PPG6 town-centre boundary; a site immediately adjacent to the primary shopping area may properly be treated as within the town centre as a matter of planning judgment, and earlier 'edge of centre' descriptions do not bind the council where retail policy analysis changed.
legal_issues: Whether Policy S2 defined the West Bridgford town centre for PPG6 purposes
Whether the council erred in treating the site as in-centre rather than edge-of-centre
Whether officer advice on local plan weight was misleading

confidence.notes: Primary ground fails clearly on plan interpretation. Subsidiary PPG1 weight point is briefly addressed.

notes: Remittal for EPDP/army release findings; Subesh standard applied but critical causation facts unresolved.

enrichment.short_title: Sri Lankan Tamil asylum remitted over EPDP release findings

statutes_considered.title: Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees 1951

key_facts: The appellant, a Sri Lankan Tamil, was allowed asylum by an adjudicator after two periods of army detention and alleged torture linked to LTTE association.
He was released from Vavuniya camp on both occasions with EPDP involvement, once reportedly after a bribe.
The IAT allowed the Secretary of State's appeal, finding he was not an exceptional 'wanted person' on return.
The Court of Appeal held neither tier had clearly resolved whether EPDP acted with or against the army and what that meant for continued risk.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Immigration Appeal Tribunal refusal of asylum and human rights claims after adjudicator allowed appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; matter remitted to a differently constituted IAT to determine whether the appellant remains wanted on return; costs to appellant subject to assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Under Subesh, the IAT may interfere with an adjudicator only if required to adopt a different view; where the critical question is whether release from army custody means the appellant is no longer wanted, and neither tribunal has made explicit findings on EPDP-army relations, remittal is necessary rather than the Court of Appeal supplying its own factual assumption.
legal_issues: Application of Subesh and Jeyachandran exceptional-case test to Sri Lankan Tamils
Whether the IAT properly addressed EPDP-orchestrated releases
Whether the appellant remained a wanted person at risk of detention and torture on return
linked_authorities: Subesh [2004] EWCA Civ 56
Jeyachandran [2002] UKIAT 01689
Selvaratnam

confidence.notes: Procedural outcome is clear but merits turn on unresolved factual findings about EPDP releases.

notes: Cohabitation declaration of trust; clause 4 contribution claim waived during lifetime is clearly decided.

enrichment.short_title: Cohabitee waived clause 4 contribution claim on joint home sale
key_facts: Julian Wade and Sheila Grimwood-Wade lived together from 1981 until her intestate death in October 1998.
They bought Forward Hoe jointly and executed a 1985 declaration of trust giving Wade 80% and the deceased 20% of net sale proceeds after mortgage and his £28,000 contribution.
Clause 4 required equal bearing of property outgoings; clause 5 fixed sale proceeds division without set-off for clause 4 balances.
After sale, Wade claimed the full proceeds or alternatively an account under clause 4; the judge declared the 20% share not reducible by clause 4.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Chancery claim for declaration on construction of declaration of trust and account under clause 4.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Wade entitled only to 80% of net proceeds; clause 4 reimbursement claim held waived during cohabitation.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 4 creates immediate mutual contribution obligations enforceable by set-off rather than deferred accounting on sale; in an informal cohabitation context, paying joint and personal outgoings without seeking contribution can impliedly waive reimbursement during the partner's lifetime, so the clause 5 share division stands.
legal_issues: Whether clauses 4 and 5 were independent or required accounting on sale
Whether payment from the joint account satisfied both parties' clause 4 obligations
Whether Wade impliedly waived reimbursement during the deceased's lifetime
Whether limitation barred any clause 4 claim
linked_authorities: Halesowen Presswork & Assemblies Ltd v Westminster Bank Ltd [1971] 1 QB 1

confidence.notes: Construction and waiver holdings are unanimous and well reasoned. Limitation point not decided.

notes: Long care judgment; residence order to maternal grandmother in Slovakia with permission to remove is the disposal.

enrichment.short_title: Child placed with maternal grandmother in Slovakia despite father's Muslim upbringing case
key_facts: A, born August 2001, was removed into care after protective police action in August 2003 following concerns about his mother's mental health and neglect.
His Slovakian Muslim-convert mother lacked capacity; his Algerian father was detained at Belmarsh facing extradition and terrorism-related allegations.
The local authority and guardian sought a residence order for the maternal grandmother with permission to remove A to Slovakia.
The father opposed removal and preferred placement with family friend Ms EH to preserve Muslim upbringing and contact.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Final welfare hearing in public law care proceedings on long-term placement and permission to remove A from the jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Residence order made in favour of the maternal grandmother with permission to remove A to Slovakia; contact orders to follow; no further assessment of the paternal uncle; local authority directed to appoint a mental health social worker for the mother.
enrichment.ratio: Where significant developmental harm from the mother's illness outweighs the father's Article 8 interests in Muslim upbringing and future contact, welfare under section 1 requires placement with the maternal grandmother in Slovakia despite risks to religious upbringing and paternal contact; a private residence order rather than a public law order is appropriate where Slovak monitoring would add no real benefit.
legal_issues: Whether A should live with the maternal grandmother in Slovakia or with Ms EH in England
Whether removal from the jurisdiction was proportionate under Article 8
Whether further assessment of Ms EH or the paternal uncle was required
Whether a public law or private law order was appropriate
index_terms: P C and S v United Kingdom
linked_authorities: Payne v Payne [2001] 1 FLR 1052
Re B (Removal from jurisdiction) [2003] 2 FLR 1043
P, C & S v United Kingdom [2002] 2 FLR 631

notes: Section 133 miscarriage-of-justice compensation appeal; saved living expenses deduction restored at 25%.

enrichment.short_title: Miscarriage-of-justice awards may deduct 25% saved living expenses
key_facts: Lord Brennan QC, Independent Assessor under section 133, assessed compensation for Michael O'Brien and Michael and Vincent Hickey after miscarriages of justice.
Maurice Kay J quashed parts of the awards on judicial review, including failure to deduct saved living expenses from loss-of-earnings components.
Lord Brennan appealed; the Hickeys cross-appealed on criminality deductions and consistency.
The Court of Appeal restored a conventional 25% deduction for saved living expenses where loss of liberty and loss of earnings were separately assessed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeals from judicial review of Independent Assessor compensation awards under section 133.
enrichment.outcome: Lord Brennan's appeal dismissed on award breakdown/aggravating features but allowed on saved living expenses; Hickey cross-appeals dismissed on criminality and consistency.
enrichment.ratio: Where a section 133 assessment separately awards loss of liberty and loss of earnings, a conventional 25% deduction for saved living expenses from the earnings component is lawful and consistent with fatal-accident and lost-years principles; Dews does not prevent such a deduction, though breakdown of non-pecuniary awards into aggravating features need not follow the judge's approach.
legal_issues: Whether awards must be broken down between loss of liberty and aggravating features
Whether saved living expenses are deductible from loss-of-earnings compensation
Whether criminality should reduce non-pecuniary awards under section 133(4A)(c)
Whether assessments lacked consistency
linked_authorities: Dews v National Coal Board [1988] AC 1
Lim v Camden Health Authority [1980] AC 174
